chapter_theme: The princes ride through the city while its women, shedding shame, pour out their longing, and in the grove under the Ashoka the Vidyadhara envoy Maruci rises, bows, studies the two princes and begins his address.

cast.role: the city's young women who love the princes
the learned envoy sent with the letter

479.reading: The poet shows the coral-lipped women of the city on its many-storeyed terraces, their bright faces and carp-like eyes playing among clusters of lotus.

480.reading: The women stand along the garlanded terraces with long spear-like eyes slanting, so that the roofs look like a lotus pool in which blue lilies have opened together.

481.reading: The women with their companions shower perfumed powder, bow with bangled forearms, lose their shame and go before the princes to beg for a garland and a glance.
481.nuance: The word கண்ணிதம்மின் is read as a plea for the princes' garland; the verse does not say it is given.
481.event: The city's women scatter perfumed powder and beg the princes for their garlands.

482.reading: In their longing the women sing and forget the tune, dance and forget the beat, leave their hair garlands unworn, and stand shy in the shade.
482.event: The women sing and dance in confusion before the princes and then draw back, shy.

483.reading: The poet praises the women's brows like two strung bows, eyes like two carp, red lips and jewelled forehead bands, and says their beauty is not only in these.

484.reading: The women gather at the long gate with lac-reddened soles and slipping girdles, so that the terraces look like a mountain where fire has scattered.
484.nuance: The comparison of the terraces to a fire-scattered mountain is hard in lines 3 and 4 and is read loosely as an image of their glow.
484.event: The women gather at the gate of the mansions, their girdles slipping.

485.reading: With anklets ringing, gold ear-rolls shining and others praising them, the women move about the gate and perform a dance for the princes.
485.event: The women dance before the princes at the gate of the mansions.

486.reading: Wearing garlands, scattering gold powder and sandal paste, the blue-eyed women give up their hearts and join the princes who rule the earth in a mist of infatuation.
486.event: The women, giving up their hearts, come to the princes.

487.reading: The women's shoulders grow pale, they sigh, their clothes slip and flowers fall from their hair, and they begin to languish as jasmine pollen scatters.
487.nuance: The verse pictures the languor of love at first sight, with no absence or parting yet; the women pine for men who have only passed.
487.event: The women, in love, grow pale and sigh.

488.reading: The troop of the princes, whose chests hold the women's eyes, bees, garlands and minds, arrives at the grove.
488.event: The troop of the princes reaches the grove.

489.reading: The women follow in heart as the kings and heroes enter the sky-high grove of flowers, and the bees, drunk on honey, rise in a swarm.
489.event: The princes and their heroes enter the grove, with the women's hearts following.

490.reading: After the elephants with golden brow-plates and white tusks are left, the bees and beetles hum at the princes as if asking whether these are the spear-bearing lovers.
490.nuance: Whether the princes dismount or the elephants simply stop is not clear from இழிந்த; read here as the princes alighting.
490.event: The princes leave their elephants and the bees gather round them.

491.reading: In the grove the madhavi creepers, as if with soft hands, show the princes the places among the flowers, while bees scatter pollen-water over them.

492.reading: The poet says the grove's colour cannot be told: flowers rain honey, bees hum, and clouds of blossoms hide the sky.
492.nuance: Lines 2 to 4 are in compressed grammar and are read only for their general sense of a grove thick with bloom.

493.reading: As the southern breeze blows through the flowering grove the vines clasp the trees, like women with garlanded hair embracing the young men they love.

494.reading: The princes pass the jasmine bowers and the madhavi arbours and reach the Ashoka tree beside the lotus bower.
494.event: The princes walk through the grove's bowers and reach the Ashoka tree.

495.reading: While the women call blessings, the princes reach the Ashoka shade and the Vidyadhara rises gladly, joins his hands and bows to them in eager love.
495.nuance: The verse says only the Vidyadhara; he is taken as Maruci, the envoy the king chose at 427 and who reached the grove at 429.
495.event: Maruci, the Vidyadhara envoy, rises and bows with joined hands to the princes under the Ashoka.

496.reading: At his bow a bright-faced prince in earrings and garland asks him why he bows to them, since they should be the ones to bow to elders of faultless virtue.
496.nuance: The verb is singular, so one prince speaks, and the verse does not say which; the id princes is used for the pair.
496.event: A prince asks Maruci why he has bowed to them.

497.reading: The Vidyadhara, come by the sky road, looks glad-eyed at one prince of milk-white radiance and one with a body like the dark sea, matching what he sees to the rules of his lore.
497.nuance: நூல்நெறி is read as the lore by which marks of a person are judged; the verse does not name the marks.
497.event: Maruci looks closely at the two princes, one fair and one dark.

498.reading: The Vidyadhara gazes at the spear-bearing heroes again and again, from their feet up to their garlands, his heart sunk in love like that of one who is lovesick.
498.nuance: The reading of காலன்கால்கள்கொண்டு கண்ணிகாறும் as 'from the feet to the garland' is uncertain; the simile of the lovesick is the poet's.
498.event: Maruci stares at the two princes from feet to garland.

499.reading: With garlands and jewels gleaming so that the eye cannot take them in, the Vidyadhara draws near the princes and, sitting on a rock beside them, begins to speak.
499.event: Maruci sits on a rock near the princes and begins to speak.

500.reading: Maruci addresses the worthy princes who came down from the golden heights, hiding the divine elephant, to humble the sea-girt earth, and says those who bow at their feet have done hard penance.
500.nuance: The speaker names no school; the claim is the envoy's courtesy. Its logic, that reaching the great is a fruit of earlier tapas, is the epic's own karma-thought, but the verse does not use the word for karma.

claims.claim: those who come to bow at the feet of the great must have done hard penance in the past

501.reading: Maruci praises the princes' radiance and the way it makes the world's beings feel gladly drawn to them, saying it cannot be matched, and goes on to hymn them.
501.nuance: Lines 1 to 3 are in compressed grammar; the sense of praise is plain but the words that carry it are not fixed.

502.reading: The princes, their gaze bright, say that talk is enough, that they will go to see their lord, and tell him to mount the elephant.
502.nuance: The word அடிகள் may name the princes' father or another lord; the verse does not say which, and the one invited to ride is read as Maruci.
502.event: The princes tell Maruci that they will go to see their lord and ask him to ride.

links.note: At 427 the ministers choose Maruci as one who can carry what he has learned and say what is fit; at 495 his first act on reaching the princes is to rise and bow.
links.teaches: The envoy named for his speech opens with a bow and not with the message, so his fitness shows first in manner.

links.note: The prince at 496 asks why the Vidyadhara bows to them; 500 gives the answer, that those who bow at their feet have done hard penance.
links.teaches: The bow is first met with surprise and then given a reason, so the envoy's courtesy is shown to rest on a belief about merit and not on mere flattery.

links.note: At 409 the astrologer's sign says Tivittan will split a lion's mouth within a month; at 497 the envoy meets the two princes and weighs them by the rules of his lore.
links.teaches: The foretold hero now meets the person who must find him, so the astrologer's sign is put to a test of eyes before the envoy speaks.

links.note: Naladiyar 17 warns against the woman's spear-like eyes, since she too will age and lean on a staff; at 486 the blue-eyed women pour out their hearts to the princes.
links.teaches: The epic shows love's pull in full while the quatrain names its price, so the two together show what a reader is warned off and why.

gains.a: A test of the women's rush of feeling against the thought that youth and beauty do not last, which the scene does not raise.
gains.b: A scene in which the beauty it warns against is shown in full, in the women's own act of giving up their hearts.

links.note: Kural 1183 says the lover has taken a woman's modesty and given her sickness and pallor; at 487 many women grow pale and sigh for men who have only passed by.
links.teaches: The Kural's single lover is replaced by two princes and a crowd, so pallor from love is shown as a common mark of beauty's reach as well as a private ache.

gains.a: A name for the paleness of the women's shoulders and a cause for it, the lover's taking of their modesty.
gains.b: A scene in which the same paleness comes at first sight of strangers, with no parting that the couplet takes as its cause.

links.note: Kural 687 ranks highest the envoy who knows the protocol, weighs the moment and place, and speaks after thought; at 500 Maruci opens with a bow and a courtesy that honours the princes before any message.
links.teaches: The epic shows an envoy meeting the Kural's test of protocol, and shows that what he first says is praise and not the matter of his errand.

gains.a: A standard that names the opening courtesy as part of the envoy's art and not a mere ornament.
gains.b: A scene in which the protocol it asks for is carried out, with praise placed ahead of the message.

source_issues: Verse 479 line 3 and 480 line 1: the edition's word division is uneven and one letter looks wrong in ந்ன்றலைந்த (479 line 4); read as நின்றலைந்த.
Verses 492, 498, 501 and 502 are in compressed grammar and are read only for their general sense.
